title: Neurulation

objective.text: Describe how the flat neural plate becomes a closed tube.

body.general: How does a flat sheet roll itself into a tube? This process, neurulation, rolls the flat neural plate into the neural tube [f1]. First the plate grows longer as its cells crowd toward the midline [f2]. Its edges rise as ridges, the neural folds, with a groove between them [f3]. The folds first meet in the future neck, beside the fifth somite [f4]. Somites are paired blocks of tissue beside the tube [f9]. From there the seam zips toward head and tail [f4]. For a while each end stays open; these openings are the neuropores [f5].
body.mbbs: Neurulation converts the neural plate into the neural tube [f1]. The plate lengthens by convergent extension, with cells moving toward the midline [f2]. Planar cell polarity signalling drives this lengthening [f2]. Its lateral edges rise as neural folds around a midline neural groove, around days 19–20 [f3]. The folds first fuse in the future neck, at about the fifth somite pair [f4]. Somites are paired blocks of paraxial mesoderm beside the tube [f9]. Fusion then proceeds both cranially and caudally, like a zip [f4]. Until closure is complete, the tube opens to the amniotic cavity through the cranial and caudal neuropores [f5].

facts.text: Neurulation turns the flat neural plate into the neural tube, which becomes the brain and spinal cord.
The plate lengthens by convergent extension, cells crowding toward the midline, driven by planar cell polarity signalling.
The plate's edges rise as neural folds around a central neural groove, around days 19–20.
The folds first meet in the neck region, at about the fifth somite, and the seam zips both toward the head and toward the tail.
facts.note: R05l first fusion site α near the hindbrain–neck junction, spreading both ways

facts.text: While closing, the tube opens to the amniotic cavity at both ends through the cranial and caudal neuropores.
Somites are paired blocks of paraxial mesoderm that form beside the neural tube.
Beyond Langman: human embryos also have a second fusion site at the front of the forebrain, which zips backward only.
Beyond Langman: the same study found no convincing sign of the mouse's extra fusion sites in humans; others dispute this.
Mutations in the planar cell polarity gene VANGL occur in some families with neural tube defects.

misconceptions.wrong: The neural tube closes all at once, or from one end.
misconceptions.right: It starts in the neck and zips both ways; the two ends (neuropores) close last.

checks.prompt: Where do the neural folds first meet?
options: Along the whole length at once
checks.why: Fusion starts near the fifth somite, in the neck region, not at one end or all along the tube at once.

checks.prompt: Put the steps of neurulation in order.
options: The neural plate lengthens toward head and tail
The plate's edges rise as neural folds around a groove
Neural folds meet in the future neck
Closure zips toward head and tail
checks.why: The plate lengthens, folds rise, they fuse first at the neck, and closure spreads toward both ends.

checks.prompt: While the tube is closing, what are the neuropores?
options: Openings at the two ends of the tube
Holes along the side of the tube
checks.why: The neuropores are the two ends of the tube, at head and tail, still open while the rest closes.

adult: The neural tube becomes the brain and spinal cord [f1].

remember.a: The neural tube, from the flat neural plate [f1].

remember.q: Where do the neural folds first fuse?
remember.a: In the neck region, about the fifth somite; then closure zips both ways [f4].
The open head and tail ends of the closing tube [f5].
